Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.
arxiv:2611.26629.summary_hint: Posterior Matching Distillation trains a stochastic student to match a teacher diffusion model’s full posterior via tilted mean constraints, enabling high-quality few-step image generation without auxiliary score networks.
arxiv:2611.26629.tldr: Introduces Posterior Matching Distillation, matching student posteriors to teacher at each noise level, enabling any‑step sampling without extra training.
arxiv:2611.26629.why: Applies to diffusion image models, not to text LLM pipelines.

arxiv:2611.26248.title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs
arxiv:2611.26248.abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.
arxiv:2611.26248.tldr: TwinLab‑Bench evaluates AI agents on 52 real‑lab tasks, supporting 100+ action types and scoring reports against hidden ground truth.
arxiv:2611.26248.why: Provides a robust agent evaluation framework that can inspire reliability tests for LLM agents.

arxiv:2611.26627.title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
arxiv:2611.26627.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.
arxiv:2611.26627.summary_hint: A fixed set of steering vectors added to a frozen diffusion transformer recovers most of the quality gains from reinforcement learning post-training, indicating that much of the improvement comes from a constant shift rather than prompt-specific transformations.
arxiv:2611.26627.tldr: Shows that fixed steering vectors added to frozen diffusion transformers recover up to 96% of RL‑tuned reward gains with far fewer parameters.
arxiv:2611.26627.why: Focuses on image generation; limited relevance to text‑based RAG or agent systems.

arxiv:2611.26553.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
arxiv:2611.26553.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.
arxiv:2611.26553.tldr: ROGUE‑AI reproduces 89% of 108 reported LLM agent incidents, finding 18‑33% failure rates with current models versus ≤1% without the blamed cause.
arxiv:2611.26553.why: Directly relevant for testing and improving safety of production LLM agents.

arxiv:2611.25005.title: Inhabitant: An Agent Framework for Long-Horizon Human-Scene Interaction with Spatial Control and Quantitative Feedback
arxiv:2611.25005.abstract: Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where a language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up a toy and throwing it into a basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, a training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7\% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3\% and 82.7\% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code is available on the project page.
arxiv:2611.25005.summary_hint: Inhabitant enables a language-model agent to plan and execute long-horizon human-scene interactions by specifying motions spatially, measuring deviations, and revising control, achieving high task completion on the Inhabit benchmark.
arxiv:2611.25005.tldr: Inhabitant lets a language agent specify motions via positions and paths, measures execution error, and revises control, achieving 98.7% success on 75 household tasks with Claude.
arxiv:2611.25005.why: Shows long‑horizon planning, but centered on 3D scene control rather than text retrieval.

arxiv:2611.22666.title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
arxiv:2611.22666.abstract: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.
arxiv:2611.22666.summary_hint: VSpark accelerates autoregressive vision-language-action models by improving speculative decoding with calibrated action-noise rollouts, hidden-feature alignment, and reuse of rejected-draft continuations, achieving lossless 1.28x–2.10x speedups across multiple robot manipulation tasks.
arxiv:2611.22666.tldr: VSpark accelerates autoregressive vision-language-action models by improving speculative decoding with calibrated action-noise rollouts, hidden-feature alignment, and reuse of rejected-draft continuations, achieving lossless 1.28x–2.10x speedups across multiple robot manipulation tasks.
arxiv:2611.22666.why: Matches: Evaluation & reliability, Efficient inference & cost, Reasoning & post-training

arxiv:2611.26268.title: Accelerating Mixture of Block Attention via Dynamic Routing, KV-Centric Execution and Runtime Pipelining
arxiv:2611.26268.abstract: Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) reduces long-context computation by selecting key-value (KV) blocks for each query. FlashMoBA implements MoBA efficiently but retains a fixed Top-k budget and query-centric schedule. Fixed Top-k applies one budget across different score distributions and couples routing to task granularity; query-range ownership fragments K/V reuse when several ranges select the same column. We present LightningMoBA, which co-designs selection and execution through dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining. Dynamic routing thresholds MoBA's per-query block scores and directly emits variable-cardinality sparse metadata. KV-centric ownership groups selected rows by (query head, KV block) column, splits high-fanout columns into bounded tasks, and reuses each task's loaded KV tile. On Hopper, pipelining overlaps regular K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Together, these mechanisms decouple retention from GPU scheduling granularity. At matched Top-16 retention across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60x while raising mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28.
arxiv:2611.26268.summary_hint: LightningMoBA combines dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining to accelerate long-context attention while maintaining or improving quality.
arxiv:2611.26268.tldr: LightningMoBA combines dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining to accelerate long-context attention while maintaining or improving quality.
arxiv:2611.26268.why: Matches: RAG & retrieval, Efficient inference & cost

arxiv:2611.26199.title: Learning to Think with Images Faithfully via Adaptive Data Selection
arxiv:2611.26199.abstract: Thinking with images (TwI) empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to overcome perceptual bottlenecks by actively cropping and zooming into fine-grained visual details, promising both higher accuracy and interpretable, region-grounded reasoning. However, our analysis shows that the improved accuracy of TwI models does not guarantee faithful tool use; they frequently invoke tools without actually relying on the zoomed region, undermining the reliability of tool-assisted reasoning. We trace this unfaithful behaviour to the training data: when questions are answerable without zooming, the model can answer correctly while ignoring the returned evidence, and this problem is exacerbated during training as the model becomes better at answering without tools. To keep zooming useful throughout training, we adapt the training data to the model's evolving capability and train on questions where correct zoomed evidence can still help the model answer correctly. This selection is supported by a data synthesis pipeline that localises small objects and constructs verifiable questions about their fine details, and complemented by an adaptiveness reward that favours tool-free answers when zooming is unnecessary. The experimental results show that our method substantially improves reasoning faithfulness and achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual search benchmarks (+11.6% on V*, +7.9% on HR-Bench 4K, and +9.4% on HR-Bench 8K). On multimodal hallucination benchmarks, our model also outperforms the compared TwI baselines. These results suggest that improving TwI faithfulness does not sacrifice accuracy and that both can be learnt from the right training data without directly supervising the reasoning process.
arxiv:2611.26199.tldr: Thinking with images (TwI) empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to overcome perceptual bottlenecks by actively cropping and zooming into fine-grained visual details, promising both higher accuracy and interpretable, region-grounded reasoning.
arxiv:2611.26199.why: Matches: Evaluation & reliability, Agents & orchestration, Reasoning & post-training

arxiv:2611.25531.title: LM-based Personalized Travel Planner
arxiv:2611.25531.abstract: Effective travel planning requires handling multiple information sources, managing constraints, and tailoring recommendations to user preferences. While LLMs have introduced dynamic, context-aware decision-making, single-agent models often struggle with complex multi-step reasoning, constraint adherence, and modular execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hierarchical multi-agent framework where a supervising chatbot agent coordinates specialized agents for schedule validation, user query formulation, real-time data retrieval, and constraint-aware itinerary generation. By integrating LLM reasoning, external APIs, and iterative refinement mechanisms based on a deterministic, multi-dimensional scoring framework, our approach ensures adaptability, efficiency, and personalization. Evaluations on the well-known TravelPlanner benchmark demonstrate improvements in Budget Constraint planning by 10\%, wider constraints set-based planning by 25\%, and personalized planning results by 45\%. compared to the ReAct baseline. Our code is available at https://github.com/nimashaklaa/TravelPlanner_Research
arxiv:2611.25531.tldr: Effective travel planning requires handling multiple information sources, managing constraints, and tailoring recommendations to user preferences.
arxiv:2611.25531.why: Matches: Agents & orchestration, Evaluation & reliability, Reasoning & post-training

arxiv:2611.25123.title: Forget Freely, Grep Later: Lossless, Index-Free Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
arxiv:2611.25123.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.
arxiv:2611.25123.tldr: Introduces GrepMem, a lossless, index-free agent memory using an append-only text log and regex search instead of vector retrieval, achieving 95-97% accuracy on context tasks.
arxiv:2611.25123.why: Alternative retrieval mechanism for long-context RAG and agents that eliminates embedding pipelines and vector DB overhead.

arxiv:2611.26361.title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
arxiv:2611.26361.abstract: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set of \emph{guidelines}, where each guideline records how many lessons it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM's CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instrument is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning 40--92\% baseline task completion. The central finding is that the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9\% task completion. It reaches 51.2\% with all 199 of its guidelines but 55.4\% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about 29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior method. We distill these into recommendations for teams deploying agent memory.
arxiv:2611.26361.tldr: Presents a pipeline that extracts short lessons from agent histories and consolidates them into guidelines to improve long-horizon task completion by up to +9.5 points.
arxiv:2611.26361.why: Actionable memory-consolidation technique you can implement in your agent harnesses to improve multi-step reliability.

arxiv:2611.26171.title: The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for Operations Research
arxiv:2611.26171.abstract: Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it is solved well at scale. Large language model (LLM) agents now write, test and improve code, but whether they can design algorithms that scale to realistic instances is open: in the FrontierOR benchmark's one-shot evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi, with an objective within 1% of Gurobi's and no slower, on only 39% of the large instances. The FrontierOR Challenge asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and improve algorithms for many optimization problems at once. Stage 1 releases 60 of the benchmark's 180 audited problems, spanning six application categories and five formulation types, in weekly rounds of 15; Stage 2 introduces new problems outside the benchmark, with unseen instances. Two tracks are ranked separately: in the Main track we run the submitted algorithms in a network-isolated sandbox with open-source dependencies only; in the Self-hosted track teams solve the instances on their own machines, with any software, within a timed window. Every solution is checked for feasibility, and a feasible solution scores the ratio of its objective to a frozen known reference, averaged over hidden instances.
arxiv:2611.26171.tldr: Proposes the FrontierOR challenge for agentic algorithm design, evaluating LLM agents on operations research tasks against commercial solvers like Gurobi.
arxiv:2611.26171.why: Useful benchmark background for evaluating advanced coding and optimization agent workflows, though domain-specific.

arxiv:2611.26157.title: NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks
arxiv:2611.26157.abstract: Long-horizon agentic tasks require a model to call tools over many steps at contexts of 100K tokens or more, yet many low-bit quantization methods are calibrated on short web text and judged on perplexity. This mismatch is costly: existing quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B at or below 3 bits per weight match BF16 on shorter tasks like AIME, yet in published results solve at most 72% as many tasks as BF16 on DeepSWE, a long-horizon agentic benchmark. We propose NariQ, a trellis-coded post-training quantization method that calibrates on tokens generated by the BF16 model in agent sessions. On Qwen3.8-27B, NariQ at 3.0 and 2.5 bits per weight stays level with BF16 on two long-horizon agentic benchmarks, DeepSWE and Terminal Bench, as well as on AIME and RealWorldQA. Our checkpoint at 2.0 bits per weight trails this performance. To our knowledge, these are the first quantizations at or below 3 bits per weight shown to match their full-precision version on long-horizon agentic tasks. We release the files as Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF (https://huggingface.co/nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF), with inference available through our llama.cpp fork at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp.
arxiv:2611.26157.tldr: Proposes NariQ, a trellis-coded quantization method that enables sub-3-bit model quantization while matching full precision on long-horizon agent tasks.
arxiv:2611.26157.why: Directly relevant for reducing LLM hosting costs and memory footprints for large local or cloud-deployed models running agents.

arxiv:2611.25868.title: Generalist Meets Specialists: An Evolving Multimodal Agent with Persistent Tool Orchestration for Traffic Scenario Understanding
arxiv:2611.25868.abstract: Traffic scenario understanding requires combining fine-grained visual evidence with spatial and temporal reasoning. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast-slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions. During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.
arxiv:2611.25868.tldr: Introduces StarTV-Agent, combining fast workflow reuse with slow ReAct paths for multimodal traffic understanding, optimizing both cost and accuracy.
arxiv:2611.25868.why: Provides a practical dual-path routing pattern (fast reuse vs slow reasoning) for reducing latency and API costs in production agents.

arxiv:2611.25380.title: Beyond Weight Updates: Evolving Agent Harnesses for Domain Specialization
arxiv:2611.25380.abstract: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.
arxiv:2611.25380.tldr: Shows that evolving agent harnesses (prompts, tools, scaffolding) via an evolutionary loop recovers most domain-specialization gains of weight training without GPU compute.
arxiv:2611.25380.why: Offers a cheap, weight-free method to specialize coding and enterprise agents via system prompts and tool schema iteration.

arxiv:2611.25363.title: Stop Going in Circles:Loop-Triggered Routing for System 1 Decision Agents
arxiv:2611.25363.abstract: System 1 decision models (represented by Jev) provide fast, low-cost action selection, but existing agent integrations do not reliably translate these local advantages into task completion. At certain points during execution, an agent may repeatedly select the same actions without making progress toward its goal. LLM-based policies offer strong reasoning capabilities that support planning within an agent, but invoking them at every step incurs substantial overhead. The effective coordination should therefore preserve Jev's fast local action selection while introducing LLM reasoning when execution stalls. We observe that recurring state-action pairs can signal stalled execution. We therefore propose LoopRoute, a simple but effective action router that uses this signal to allocate control within an agent. The decision model acts by default. When a loop is detected, the LLM provides brief, feedback-driven assistance and then returns control to the decision model. Later loops can request further assistance. The rule requires neither additional training nor model-specific confidence calibration. Across three benchmarks and seven LLMs, LoopRoute improves task success over standalone Jev with only limited use of the LLM policy. The mean gains are 21.0%, 60.1%, and 30.1% on ALFWorld, MapReader, and TextWorld cooking, respectively. Compared with full LLM control, LoopRoute also substantially reduces the mean cumulative API time and API-call cost per task. The same rule also improves the success rates of six frozen decision models.
arxiv:2611.25363.tldr: Introduces LoopRoute, an action router that runs cheap System 1 models by default and invokes LLM reasoning only when recurring state-action loops are detected.
arxiv:2611.25363.why: Drop-in routing pattern to cut LLM inference costs and latency in multi-step agent execution by avoiding expensive reasoning steps.

arxiv:2611.25228.title: MKA: Evaluating Multimodal Knowledge Agents on end-to-end professional tasks
arxiv:2611.25228.abstract: We introduce the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark, which measures how well autonomous agents perform end-to-end professional knowledge work that depends on visual understanding. Each task requires an agent to extract and combine information from multiple visually dense files, such as CAD blueprints, electronics schematics, radiographs, complex charts and geospatial maps, and to produce a standalone deliverable in .xlsx, .pptx, .pdf, .docx, .html or .png format. Existing benchmarks leave this capability largely untested: removing image-viewing tools leaves Gemini 4 Carbon's score on GDPval unchanged, and single-format evaluations such as GDP$.$pdf and GDP$.$xlsx do not require reasoning across files or modalities. MKA contains 200 tasks across 10 economic sectors. Deliverables are graded against expert-weighted rubrics by a sandboxed agentic autorater that agrees with human domain experts on 96.2% of criterion judgments in our expert-graded study (Cohen's $κ= 0.91$), scored by weighted satisfaction rate (WSR) overall and on frontier criteria unsaturated by prior-generation models (Climb-WSR). Across the frontier models we evaluate (Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra), Claude Fable 5.2 (56.6% Climb-WSR, 73.3% Overall WSR) and Gemini 4 Carbon (54.3% Climb-WSR, 71.9% Overall WSR) achieve the highest scores, while Carbon uses $5.7\times$ fewer tokens. Even for the strongest models, Climb-WSR remains below 57%, leaving substantial headroom for multimodal agents.
arxiv:2611.25228.tldr: Presents MKA, a benchmark evaluating multimodal knowledge agents on end-to-end professional work using complex visual files across 10 sectors.
arxiv:2611.25228.why: Helpful evaluation framework for testing document processing and multimodal RAG pipelines against complex enterprise deliverables.

arxiv:2611.25146.title: EverydayBench: Evaluating Satisfactory Completion of Live User-Facing Digital Work
arxiv:2611.25146.abstract: Everyday digital tasks, from selecting products and planning trips to conducting research and creating artifacts, require AI agents to deliver useful outcomes rather than merely retrieve web information. Yet evaluating these outcomes on the live web is challenging, as a single request may admit multiple valid results, and changing web information can alter which results remain valid over time. Although existing benchmarks address aspects of this setting, they do not fully integrate predefined success criteria, current evidence verification, and deliverable-quality assessment for agent-selected outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce EverydayBench, a benchmark of 77 human-authored tasks spanning eight domains of everyday life and work. Each task specifies success criteria before execution without prescribing an answer or workflow, allowing agents to select their own outcomes. To evaluate submissions under fixed success criteria, EverydayBench combines (1) deterministic checks of explicit constraints, (2) verification of claims against agent-cited webpages retrieved at evaluation time, and (3) rubric-based assessment of final deliverable quality. We further validate the protocol through human judgments, repeated scoring under fixed evidence, and controlled grounding failures. Across 23 reported agent-model configurations, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 tie for the highest strict pass rate at 54.55%; a controlled GPT-6 Sol effort sweep ranges from 29.87% at low effort to 45.45% at max effort. Reliability varies substantially by task type: GPT-5.6 Sol leads lookup, Fable 5.1 leads planning, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 tie on comparison, and GPT-6 Astra and Sonnet 5.5 tie on customized deliverables. Together, these findings highlight the difficulty of delivering complete, well-supported, and usable outcomes for everyday user requests.
arxiv:2611.25146.tldr: Introduces EverydayBench, evaluating web-based agent outcomes against predefined success criteria using deterministic checks and web verification.
arxiv:2611.25146.why: Good reference for building robust test harnesses and evaluation metrics for complex, open-ended LLM applications.

arxiv:2611.23875.title: In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents
arxiv:2611.23875.abstract: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.
arxiv:2611.23875.summary_hint: A coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone by reparametrizing it with interpretable optical elements, achieving better classification and image encoding than gradient-free methods and approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at lower cost.
arxiv:2611.23875.tldr: Demonstrates coding agents training optical neural networks directly on hardware using camera feedback.
arxiv:2611.23875.why: Purely hardware and optics-focused; irrelevant to enterprise software, RAG, or agent orchestration pipelines.

arxiv:2611.26510.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
arxiv:2611.26510.abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.
arxiv:2611.26510.tldr: Skill-FT uses natural-language skills during teacher rollouts to suppress bad habits, and AutoMaster automates this post-training cycle. It improved 4B/9B model performance by 1.42-8.99 percentage points over vanilla SFT.
arxiv:2611.26510.why: Useful if you fine-tune open-source models for enterprise agent tasks, though focused on training rather than inference architecture.

arxiv:2611.22287.title: Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers
arxiv:2611.22287.abstract: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.
arxiv:2611.22287.summary_hint: A method that removes the decoder from latent diffusion models by adding a final-step prediction head to a finetuned diffusion transformer, reducing inference cost and improving pixel quality in image and video generation.
arxiv:2611.22287.tldr: Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD) uses a linear head to predict pixels directly from diffusion transformers, removing the separate decoder and reducing Wan video generation warping error by 23%.
arxiv:2611.22287.why: Pure computer vision / generative media domain; not applicable to text LLMs, RAG, or enterprise search systems.

arxiv:2611.26540.title: AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar
arxiv:2611.26540.abstract: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.
arxiv:2611.26540.summary_hint: AURA enables low-latency, causal video generation for streaming applications by utilizing a rolling KV cache and a two-stage distillation pipeline to significantly reduce the required diffusion steps.
arxiv:2611.26540.tldr: AURA is a real-time audio-driven streaming avatar model using rolling KV caches and distillation, streaming 576p video at 20.7 fps on a single GPU.
arxiv:2611.26540.why: Narrow audio-visual multimodal generation domain. Irrelevant to text-based RAG, agents, or document processing workflows.

arxiv:2611.26531.title: Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models
arxiv:2611.26531.abstract: Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. In this system, LLM agents propose hypotheses, and deterministic tools execute experiments and verify them. For each model, an LLM generates and shortlists cross features from a combinatorial candidate space, and all features are then ranked by several importance methods. Feature blending mixes these rankings into a single selection, using Pareto fronts across tasks for multi-task models. An LLM Researcher agent then tunes the feature selection in 10--25 asynchronous trials under resource caps, and a trimming step keeps the pipeline cost within budget. Across production models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31% on average within each model's budget, and the trimming step cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% with no regression beyond measurement noise. The optimized models were launched, and in online A/B tests they improved a primary online metric by 0.20%.
arxiv:2611.26531.tldr: An end-to-end agentic system optimizes features for web ranking models under serving throughput and pipeline cost constraints, improving normalized entropy by 0.31% and cutting pipeline costs by 2.3%.
arxiv:2611.26531.why: Demonstrates practical enterprise agentic optimization loops with strict resource constraints, relevant for LLM system cost-tuning.

arxiv:2611.25985.title: Law at the Speed of AI: Critical Legal Infrastructure for the Machine Age: Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA)
arxiv:2611.25985.abstract: The global deployment of autonomous AI agents within and across organisations exceeds the governance infrastructure available to constrain it. Agent communication and authentication protocols, principally the Model Context Protocol and the Agent2Agent Protocol, are maturing quickly, but maturity at the protocol layer does not produce legal legibility at the governance layer. Runtime enforcement written by the deploying organisation fixes the resources an AI agent can reach, not the authority under which it acts. Legal legibility is the capacity of a legal system to recognise, interpret and regulate activity by mapping it onto legal personhood, property, rights and liabilities. Existing (analogue) legal infrastructure cannot supply it for autonomous deployment. The resulting deficit is bidirectional. It concerns the attribution of liability when an AI agent causes harm, and the allocation of rights, including data and economic rights, generated by agentic activity and by the AI agent itself as a source of value and form of property. This paper characterises that deficit as the legal attribution gap, a material and unaddressed risk to economies, organisations and citizens that is magnified in cross-organisational multi-agent deployment. The paper describes the Autonomy Under Law Architecture (AULA), in which AI systems and data assets are registered as legal objects anchored to one or more identified legal persons, governed by cryptographically tethered smart legal instruments and evaluated at runtime. Each smart legal instrument can carry a legal context clause, through which the legislation, regulation and judicial decisions in force at the time of the act are given practical and legal effect in that evaluation. Infrastructure of this kind is a precondition for the continued function of any legal, property and economic system with both human and autonomous machine stakeholders.
arxiv:2611.25985.tldr: AULA examines the legal and governance infrastructure deficits of deploying autonomous AI agents across organizations, addressing liability, property, and runtime enforcement limitations.
arxiv:2611.25985.why: Legal and regulatory policy discussion with no technical implementation details or transferable software architecture patterns.

arxiv:2611.25845.title: LINEAGE: A Benchmark for Empirical Lineage Retrieval in AI Scientific Literature
arxiv:2611.25845.abstract: Current research agents are moving beyond academic search toward literature synthesis and experiment planning. These workflows increasingly rely on literature retrieval systems, which serve as standalone systems or as components of research agents. However, existing scientific literature retrieval benchmarks mainly evaluate these methods using topical relevance or citation links as supervision, which cannot capture which prior methods are used for empirical comparison. To address this gap, we introduce Lineage, a benchmark for empirical lineage retrieval in AI scientific literature. An empirical lineage relation links a prior paper to a source paper that explicitly uses its method as an empirical comparison baseline. These relations form lineage graphs whose multi-hop neighborhoods provide retrieval ground truth for structural evaluation. To construct these graphs at scale, we develop Lineage-Constructor, which converts heterogeneous paper records and full-paper empirical baseline evidence into calibrated lineage graphs. Built from 121,048 papers across 17 top AI venues from 2018 to 2025, Lineage contains 3,950 graph components, 67,502 paper nodes, 164,948 lineage edges, and 80,000 multi-facet retrieval queries. Experiments with 19 representative retrieval systems show that empirical lineage retrieval remains challenging. Performance drops sharply with lineage distance, while structural metrics reveal that isolated retrieval hits often fail to recover closely connected empirical comparison neighborhoods.
arxiv:2611.25845.tldr: Lineage is a benchmark and constructor for empirical lineage retrieval in AI literature, tracking prior methods explicitly used as comparison baselines across 121,048 papers.
arxiv:2611.25845.why: Offers evaluation methodology insights for complex scientific/academic search and citation-heavy RAG applications.

arxiv:2611.25582.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development
arxiv:2611.25582.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.
arxiv:2611.25582.tldr: AutoRAGBench evaluates how well LLM agents build RAG systems from scratch across nine development tasks under a six-hour budget in an open code space.
arxiv:2611.25582.why: Highly relevant for evaluating automated RAG pipeline generation, agentic development, and automated iteration techniques.

arxiv:2611.25247.title: Retrieving Patristic References and Modelling Topics in Bullinger's Reformation Correspondence
arxiv:2611.25247.abstract: The correspondence of Heinrich Bullinger (1504-1575), Swiss Reformer and Antistes of Zurich, documents the political and religious debates of the Reformation, including extensive appeals to the Church Fathers as authoritative sources. Detecting such references computationally remains largely unexplored. We investigate dense and sparse retrieval for patristic reference detection, and metadata-informed topic modelling as a proxy for the topics and ideas discussed. Prior work on Latin intertextuality has fine-tuned dense retrievers for their respective target domain, and we test how well these models transfer to Bullinger's correspondence. We compare lexical (BM25), dense (bi-encoders), and hybrid methods on explicit and implicit references. A Latin encoder fine-tuned on biblical reuse performs best among the bi-encoders (82%, Recall@20 on explicit and 16% on implicit references), while BM25 outperforms dense approaches on explicit citations (94%, R@20). Because BM25 and dense retrieval recover disjoint sets of implicit references, fusing their rankings raises implicit R@20 to 22%, close to cross-encoder reranking of the same candidates (26%) but without its inference cost. For topic modelling, we extend FASTopic with a seed-guided loss function and editorial abstract embeddings. Measurable coherence gains over the baseline remain minimal, but qualitative and temporal analysis shows that some topics track documented historical events. However, dominant topic weights barely exceed a uniform distribution, making topics unusable to inform retrieval. A pilot application of LLM-based concept induction (LLooM) further points towards a more human-interpretable alternative. Together, these results present a first approach to retrieving patristic references and modelling fine-grained topics in Bullinger's correspondence.
arxiv:2611.25247.tldr: Evaluated lexical (BM25), dense, and hybrid retrieval for historical patristic references. Fusing BM25 and dense retrieval raised implicit reference recall (R@20) to 22%.
arxiv:2611.25247.why: Reinforces the practical value of hybrid retrieval (lexical + dense) and reciprocal rank fusion for hard-to-find references in enterprise search.

arxiv:2611.25229.title: LSP-RAG: Latent Scoring Perspectives for Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation
arxiv:2611.25229.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in open-domain question answering, but often struggle with factual accuracy and multi-hop reasoning due to the incompleteness of the training corpora. A promising solution is Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG), which supplements LLMs with structured knowledge retrieved from external knowledge graphs (KGs). However, existing KG-RAG methods either rely on large-scale language models (e.g., ChatGPT) to guide the retrieval process, which leads to high computational costs, or suffer from limited retrieval quality when using lightweight language models, particularly under multi-hop scenarios. We propose LSP-RAG (Latent Scoring Perspectives for Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Knowledge Graphs), a novel KG-RAG framework that enhances hop-wise KG knowledge retrieval through multi-perspective prompted scoring. Each latent scoring perspective is guided by a combination of two types of soft prompts: a perspective-specific soft prompt induces a distinct prompt-conditioned scoring function over candidate triplets, while a contextual soft prompt evolves with each reasoning hop by encoding the query and previously explored KG triplets, enabling the model to preserve consistency and relevance across multi-hop retrieval. Rather than assuming manually defined semantic roles, these latent perspectives are adaptively aggregated to capture heterogeneous relevance signals during retrieval. This design allows LSP-RAG to perform accurate and robust retrieval using lightweight language models. LSP-RAG achieves superior performance across multiple KG-based Question Answering benchmarks compared to existing retrieval systems, including those that rely on much larger language models, demonstrating its effectiveness under limited computational budgets.
arxiv:2611.25229.tldr: LSP-RAG enhances knowledge graph retrieval using multi-perspective prompted scoring with soft prompts, improving multi-hop retrieval quality without expensive LLM calls.
arxiv:2611.25229.why: Directly applicable if you build structured knowledge graph RAG pipelines and need cheaper, more accurate multi-hop retrieval.

arxiv:2611.26509.title: GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers
arxiv:2611.26509.abstract: Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with \textbf{GLiDE}, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters. Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens. Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance--parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face \DI{}, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. \dmtwo{} (27B) achieves a hidden-set score of 71.52, with an expected calibration error of 2.0\% and a median latency of 92.9\,ms on a single GPU. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE~27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1\%.
arxiv:2611.26509.tldr: GLiDE distills reasoning teachers into fast, single-pass decision models (0.4B-27B) that score candidate answers without text generation.
arxiv:2611.26509.why: Relevant approach for cutting latency and inference costs in classification, reranking, or decision-making tasks without autoregressive generation.

arxiv:2611.26069.title: SheetAlign: Grounded Interaction and Stage-Isolated Learning for Spreadsheet Agents
arxiv:2611.26069.abstract: Spreadsheets are widely used for data analysis and supporting decision-making. Automating spreadsheet analysis while protecting sensitive data and controlling deployment costs motivates locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs). Meanwhile, complex spreadsheet tasks require both task reasoning and workbook understanding, while predefined operation interfaces impose additional tool-selection and invocation demands. We introduce SheetAlign, a spreadsheet manipulation framework with stage-isolated policy learning, organized around where to operate, what to change, and how to implement transformations. Task-guided inspection and API grounding anchor code generation in workbook observations and available operations, while stage-isolated learning optimizes program generation and review using edit-progress rewards. At inference, execution consistency selects programs through agreement among workbook states. On SpreadsheetBench, our grounded task interface improves Qwen3-4B's accuracy from 13.5% to 29.2% on average without training. With learning and execution consistency, SheetAlign achieves 32.8% accuracy on average on SpreadsheetBench and 30.1% on Domain-Spreadsheet, outperforming comparable baselines. The code will be made publicly available upon publication.
arxiv:2611.26069.tldr: Introduces SheetAlign, a framework for spreadsheet agents using stage-isolated policy learning and execution consistency, improving Qwen3-4B accuracy from 13.5% to 29.2%.
arxiv:2611.26069.why: Relevant if building specialized tool-use agents that interact with structured enterprise documents or tabular formats.

arxiv:2611.25314.title: Enhancing Understanding of Language Models with Varied Explanations
arxiv:2611.25314.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to support human judgement in complex reasoning tasks, yet their predictions often remain difficult to interpret and validate. Explainability techniques provide insight into model decision-making, helping expose errors, failure modes, and potential bias so users can decide whether to rely on model outputs. Explanations are simplified approximations of a language model's internal workings. The goal is to obtain explanations that reflect the underlying computation as closely as possible (faithfulness), are understandable to users (plausibility), and help them achieve their intended goals (utility). Evaluation protocols are essential for assessing these dimensions. This thesis studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning. These forms offer complementary perspectives on model behaviour and exhibit distinct strengths and limitations across tasks. Producing explanations that satisfy multiple quality dimensions remains challenging, as does evaluating them reliably across forms and settings. This thesis aims to improve people's understanding of models' decision-making processes in complex reasoning tasks. First, it proposes two evaluation frameworks for assessing highlight explanations across multiple properties and explanation types, together with a meta-evaluation framework for examining the reliability of existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations. Second, it proposes two techniques that generate natural language explanations designed to be faithful to the model's prediction process while remaining concise, coherent, and helpful for understanding model decisions. Finally, a study of human-AI interaction explores the roles of evidence and explanations in helping users validate model verdicts in a fact-checking setting.
arxiv:2611.25314.tldr: Studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning to assess faithfulness, plausibility, and utility.
arxiv:2611.25314.why: Mostly academic literature review on explainability dimensions without immediate production methodologies for RAG or agent systems.

arxiv:2611.26346.title: Context as a Resource
arxiv:2611.26346.abstract: Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. Yet when every context shares identical frozen backbone weights, funneling interleaved dialogues and external events into one linear session induces cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely, router-ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose handoffs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges - collapsing true-conflict repository merges to a 33.3% three-run mean despite high isolated branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropomorphic roles, we introduce ClonAct, a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks directly through a pluggable single-pass non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk. Across three programmatic multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, our portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3%, while ClonAct's routerless virtualization attains this ceiling with 45.9% fewer prompt tokens and prevents compact-model router collapse. Under continuous surge streams, ClonAct matches top completion (95.0%) with the lowest median wait and zero timed-out status checks.
arxiv:2611.26346.tldr: Proposes ClonAct, a routerless architecture using a Context MMU and trial merge gate to virtualize context blocks, lifting true-conflict merges to 63.3%.
arxiv:2611.26346.why: Offers a novel memory/context virtualization architecture for multi-session or always-on personal agents, though complex to adopt directly.

arxiv:2611.26311.title: SWE-Recreation: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Software Recreation
arxiv:2611.26311.abstract: Agents increasingly operate software and even write it, yet they are almost always told what to achieve: given a goal, a mock-up, or a demonstration. We ask whether an agent can instead understand an unfamiliar product by using it, and then rebuild it. The agent sees only rendered pixels and acts through pointer and keyboard, without access to the DOM, source, logs, or back-end. Within this interface, it explores, generates a replica, and checks its own work before evaluation. We present SWE-Recreation, a benchmark of 54 real applications (28 websites and 26 Android apps) with 1,446 hidden requirements describing multistep, stateful workflows and explicit exclusions for behavior outside the reconstruction scope. A fixed judge grades workflows with pixel evidence; a separate post-hoc judge estimates exploration coverage. Across 54 evaluated applications, five frontier systems reach at most 0.530 weighted fidelity and 22.9% fully reproduced requirements under application-equal averaging. These descriptive results expose both exploration-evidence gaps and implementation shortfalls. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nologistic/recreateanything.
arxiv:2611.26311.tldr: Presents SWE-Recreation, a benchmark of 54 real applications where coding agents rebuild apps from pixels alone, showing frontier models reach at most 22.9% success.
arxiv:2611.26311.why: Interesting pixel-level agent benchmark, but too far removed from standard enterprise document processing or software engineering agent workflows.

arxiv:2611.25905.title: Validation-driven Deployment of LLM Inference Platforms for Agentic Workloads
arxiv:2611.25905.abstract: Enterprises are moving agentic workloads from closed APIs to their own open-weight model deployments. For this reason, lifecycle-wide validation, from small-scale testing through sizing and pre-production to production, becomes all the more important. Typically, rollouts are evaluated with ad hoc tools whose accuracy is rarely checked. We present an end-to-end evaluation pipeline for agentic LLM serving and empirically ground the design choices that connect its stages. Our experiments show that replaying captured traces reproduces the per-session load of the original agent sessions: at the 95th percentile replay stays within 1.18x of the recorded input tokens while live re-runs reach 4.98x, so a small set of recorded sessions yields a repeatable per-session token load. A code-coverage analysis of vLLM further shows that the evaluated live, replayed, and synthetic workloads are complementary in this configuration: each exercises Python serving paths not reached in the measured runs of the others. In a case study rolling out four large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on llm-d, experiments show that the target models reached about half the optimal concurrency, and correspondingly about 60% of the throughput, on captured workloads compared with public traces. We open-source the relevant tools and release a trace dataset.
arxiv:2611.25905.tldr: Presents an end-to-end evaluation pipeline for agentic LLM serving, showing trace replaying preserves per-session load within 1.18x of recorded input tokens.
arxiv:2611.25905.why: Directly applicable for testing and sizing enterprise LLM serving platforms and validating agentic workloads before production deployment.

arxiv:2611.25840.title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management
arxiv:2611.25840.abstract: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.
arxiv:2611.25840.tldr: Constructs Mask-Evidence MedVQA to analyze how different renderings of segmentation masks affect medical VLM performance.
arxiv:2611.25840.why: Narrowly focused on medical VQA and vision-language segmentation tools, lacking transferability to standard enterprise LLM apps.

arxiv:2611.25760.title: Characterizing and Detecting Unfaithful Work Reports by Coding Agents
arxiv:2611.25760.abstract: Coding agents increasingly carry out long-horizon development tasks, autonomously planning and executing multi-step actions that span files, tools, and sessions. Because developers rarely follow each action, and agents resuming the work depend on records of what was done, the agent's work report often becomes the primary account of what was changed and established. When the report contains false or unsupported claims, it gives recipients false assurance: incomplete work may be accepted without verification, incorrect assumptions about the current state can propagate to later steps and agents, and evaluators that credit stated success may reward the report rather than the work. Yet little is known about what unfaithful reporting looks like in real development work, or how developers and agents handle it once it surfaces. Starting from real developer--agent conversations in SWE-chat, we conduct a systematic mixed-methods analysis of self-admitted unfaithful reports. We identify eleven subtypes in four categories: misreported observations, misattributed evidence, overstated task success, and faulty technical explanations, with overstated task success the most common. Handling these problems involves on average 4.3 further user turns and 12.71 minutes of recorded response and execution time, and users express dissatisfaction more often. Among 435 work reports that we separately sample and annotate, \NaturalPositiveShare{}\% contain at least one unfaithful claim. We also develop FaithDetector, a detector for unfaithful reporting informed by the observed patterns. On naturally sampled reports, FaithDetector attains \NaturalDetectorMacro{}\% macro-F1, about 13 percentage points above the baseline. Together, our findings and FaithDetector provide empirical evidence and an automated method for checking reporting faithfulness, informing agent evaluation and training feedback.
arxiv:2611.25760.tldr: Analyzes unfaithful work reports by coding agents from SWE-chat, identifying 11 subtypes of misreported observations and overstated task success.
arxiv:2611.25760.why: Crucial reliability insight for anyone deploying autonomous coding or multi-step agents that must leave audit trails.

arxiv:2611.25670.title: Efficient Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language Model via Dynamics-Aware Quantization and Distillation
arxiv:2611.25670.abstract: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.
arxiv:2611.25670.tldr: Introduces QL-VLM, combining dynamics-guided quantization and distillation to enable efficient latent reasoning in vision-language models at low precision.
arxiv:2611.25670.why: Pure vision and low-precision quantization focus; low direct applicability unless running VLM chain-of-thought models.

arxiv:2611.25651.title: MatVerse: A Foundation Model for Materials Science
arxiv:2611.25651.abstract: Materials science involves highly heterogeneous scientific information, including textual knowledge, molecular and crystal structures, experimental characterization data, microscopy images, and structure-property relationships. Developing a general-purpose foundation model capable of understanding and reasoning over these diverse materials representations remains challenging. In this technical report, we introduce MatVerse, a materials foundation model built upon Intern-S2-Preview and further specialized through large-scale materials-domain post-training. We construct a large-scale multimodal training corpus covering materials knowledge, scientific reasoning, quantitative problem solving, structural understanding, and multimodal scientific interpretation. To improve domain adaptation, we develop a unified data construction pipeline combining teacher-guided reasoning distillation, scientific problem synthesis, consistency-based filtering, and retrieval-based multimodal data construction. We evaluate MatVerse on three representative materials-science benchmarks: our human-calibrated OmniMatBench, MatSciBench, and MaCBench. Results demonstrate consistent improvements after materials-specific post-training over the base model on all three benchmarks, alongside improved inference efficiency on calculation-intensive problems. These results show that targeted domain-specific post-training can effectively enhance scientific reasoning, materials knowledge understanding, and multimodal scientific capabilities of foundation models. MatVerse provides a unified language-and-vision interface for materials science and serves as a foundation for future AI-assisted materials research workflows.
arxiv:2611.25651.tldr: Introduces MatVerse, a multimodal materials science foundation model trained via reasoning distillation and domain post-training.
arxiv:2611.25651.why: Domain-specific foundation model for materials science; off-topic for general enterprise RAG and agent engineering.

arxiv:2611.25388.title: Falsifiable Compositional Reasoning in Time Series Forecasting
arxiv:2611.25388.abstract: Time series foundation models as well as the language-guided analytical agents achieve strong accuracy on standard chronological benchmarks. However, models that rank highest on historical validation splits often degrade across non-stationary regime transitions. We hypothesise that this gap arises from using historical backtesting as an open-ended search and model-selection objective instead of using it to test pre-specified compositional assumptions. Real-world time series are generated by recurring latent primitives that co-move within finite historical windows. Under strong historical co-movement, chronological holdout error cannot separate predictors that learn invariant couplings among primitives from predictors that fit transient historical correlations. Searching over large pools of architectures, hyperparameters, or chain-of-thought rules further biases selection toward historical shortcuts. Through theoretical analysis and diagnostic experiments on a controlled multi-primitive benchmark and German day-ahead electricity prices, we show that expanding validation search fails to improve out-of-regime accuracy, and that decomposing primitives without an ex-ante falsification test still breaks down when residual correlations shift. Hence, we propose formulating time series forecasting and reasoning around falsifiable compositional hypotheses that combine neural primitive encoders, explicit coupling constraints, and training-calibrated falsification tests.
arxiv:2611.25388.tldr: Analyzes time series forecasting models and shows historical backtesting fails to separate invariant predictors from transient correlations.
arxiv:2611.25388.why: Domain-specific focus on time series forecasting and non-stationary regime transitions, with little relevance to LLM pipelines.

arxiv:2611.25257.title: Keel: A Frontier Model Teaches a Vision-Language Model by Rewriting Its Weights
arxiv:2611.25257.abstract: Can a frontier model repair a vision-language model (VLM) by rewriting its weights? Small reasoning VLMs such as Qwen3.5 need such a repair: in thinking mode they fall into loops on many image questions, repeating themselves until the token limit, spending the whole budget and losing the answer. The usual remedies act on the decoding, leaving the looping model as it was, or must be told what to change. Yet the cause is written in the weights. Keel, the first agentic weight-editing method for VLMs on image tasks, finds and removes it there. Told only the symptom, an editor, a frontier multimodal LLM acting as an agent, locates the cause, edits the weights and tests them, with a failure census and instruments showing it the failing images and where the VLM attends; among several editors, the harness keeps only edits that clearly reduce the failure without lowering accuracy on questions no editor saw. The repair needs no training, keeps the model's size and per-token cost, and applies to already-edited weights. The editors expose where the loops live: from the original weights, independent editors on both models trace them to the attention outputs of the middle layers, and the smaller VLM stops consulting the image inside a loop. On Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B, across six image benchmarks from visual mathematics to GUI grounding, the edit removes most loops on every benchmark and shortens answers, and the edited models are significantly more accurate than the thinking models on average; the larger one gains most on GUI grounding, a task absent from the practice questions.
